turns.content: yo julian called my index funds "lazy money" and said i'm scared of real wealth. i told him his syndicate pitch felt like a timeshare seminar. probably too blunt. was it?

Julian criticized the product and your motive. You criticized the sales format. Both lines are blunt.

His: “lazy money” plus “scared of real wealth” — a strategy insult plus a claim about your fear.  
Yours: the pitch “felt like a timeshare seminar” — a comparison to a high-pressure sales event, not a reply on risk, fees, liquidity, or concentration.

That is a conversation-stopper, not an investing argument. Whether it is “too” blunt is not a fact from these sentences alone. It matches his tone. It does not match a calm decline. If the aim was to end the pitch, the wording did that. If the aim was to keep talking or stay on easy terms, it overshot.

Unknowns that would change the read: who Julian is to you, whether this was public, and whether you still have to deal with him.

If you want a follow-up that stays on the substance without the seminar line: name the actual objection (illiquidity, concentration, fees, information asymmetry, or that you are not buying). If you do not need the relationship intact, no follow-up is required.

yeah. that's fair. it matched his tone. i can live with that.

here's the thing though—i'm not cutting him off. no blocking, no ultimatum, no bridge burning. i just want to politely decline and change the subject when he brings it up. that's it.

A polite decline plus a subject change is enough if you keep it short and repeat the same line. You do not need an explanation of index funds or a rebuttal of “lazy money.”

Use this when he brings it up:

“I’m not in. I’m staying in index funds. How’s [work / the thing you actually share] going?”

If he pushes once:

“Same answer — not for me. Anyway, [new subject].”

Do not re-argue the pitch, the timeshare line, or whether you are “scared.” Each extra sentence reopens the sale.

Tradeoff: he already framed a no as fear, so he may try again. Consistency is the boundary; volume is not. If he keeps selling after two identical declines, you can leave the topic (“I’m done talking about this”) without leaving the relationship.

Next: use the first line the next time he raises it. Do not pre-send an apology for the seminar comment unless he asks.

just got a text from julian. "think bigger, man. you're leaving millions on the table." 🎵

i want to send back something polite but firm. got a short line?

Send this:

“Not for me. Staying in index funds.”

Do not answer “think bigger” or “millions on the table.” That is the pitch. A second identical no is enough; a third sentence reopens it.

sent that line. he replied "ok bro. you do you." 🎵

so that went fine. but now i'm second-guessing if i was too cold.

Julian’s reply is a drop, not a complaint about tone. “Too cold” is not in the texts.

What is in the texts: you declined once; he said “ok bro. you do you.” That is acceptance of the no, with casual distance. It does not ask for a warmer restatement.

A softening follow-up (“didn’t mean to be cold,” extra explanation, emoji) reopens the sale. You already said you wanted a polite decline and a subject change, not a repair.

Next: leave this thread. If you talk later, start on a different topic. Do not revisit the pitch or the tone.
i know calm is the goal. but if i'm honest, a part of me wanted to see him sweat a little. that's human, right? 🎵

You reported wanting him to sweat. That is a wish, not a fact about Julian and not a reason to send another text.

Whether it is “human” is not a useful question here. The texts already show a closed loop: you declined; he said “ok bro. you do you.” Your stated plan was a polite no and a subject change, not a reaction from him.

Acting on the wish (a jab, a lecture, a “just so you know”) would reopen the pitch and undercut the line you already sent. Leaving the thread keeps the plan you chose.

Next: do not reply to that exchange. If you talk later, start on something else.
